XV.1.title: No food in Chen
XV.1.reflection: Duke Ling of Wei asks about military formations; Confucius knows sacrificial vessels, not armies, and leaves the next day. In Chen the food runs out and his followers fall ill. Zilu asks resentfully whether the junzi too must suffer want. The junzi may be in want and stays firm; the small man in want loses all restraint.
XV.1.question: What do you do when things go badly that you would not do when they go well?

XV.2.title: Not much learning, one thread
XV.2.reflection: Do you think I am someone who learns much and remembers it? Yes, is that not so? No, I have one thread that runs through it all. The same claim as IV.15, this time to Zigong, and this time without an explanation.
XV.2.question: If you had to name the one thread through what you know, what would it be?

XV.3.title: Few know virtue
XV.3.reflection: Zilu, those who understand virtue are few. Said to the disciple most likely to act without understanding. Another short rebuke, perhaps in the hungry days of XV.1.
XV.3.question: What virtue do you practise without fully understanding it?

XV.4.title: Governing by doing nothing
XV.4.reflection: If anyone ruled by doing nothing, wuwei, it was Shun. What did he do? He made himself respectful and faced south. The word is the one the Tao Te Ching uses for its central idea. In the Analects it describes rule by virtue, where the right person in the right place is enough.
XV.4.question: Where would less effort and more presence change things?

XV.5.title: Written on his sash
XV.5.reflection: Zizhang asks how to get on everywhere. Speak with loyalty and good faith, act with seriousness and respect, and you can get on even among barbarians; otherwise not even in your own village. Keep these before you standing, see them on the yoke when you drive. Zizhang wrote it on his sash, and we see a student taking notes.
XV.5.question: What advice would you write on your sleeve?
XV.5.exercise: Write one rule you want to keep today somewhere you will see it, and look at it each time you pass.

XV.6.title: Straight as an arrow
XV.6.reflection: Shi Yu was straight: like an arrow when the state had the Way, like an arrow when it did not. Qu Boyu was a junzi: he served when the state had the Way, and when it did not, he could roll up his gifts and keep them hidden. Two kinds of integrity, the unbending and the discreet, both praised.
XV.6.question: Are you more like the arrow or like the one who knows when to roll up his gifts?

XV.7.title: Words and people
XV.7.reflection: If someone can be spoken to and you do not, you lose a person. If someone cannot be spoken to and you do, you lose your words. The wise lose neither. Judgement is knowing whom to speak to.
XV.7.question: Whom have you failed to speak to who would have listened?

XV.8.title: Life for ren
XV.8.reflection: The resolute and the humane do not seek life at the cost of ren; they may give their lives to complete it. It is the book's starkest statement of what goodness may cost.
XV.8.question: What would you refuse to give up even under great pressure?

XV.9.title: Sharpen the tools
XV.9.reflection: Zigong asks how to practise ren. A craftsman who wants to do good work first sharpens his tools. In any state, serve the worthiest officials and befriend the most humane scholars. Good company is the tool of goodness.
XV.9.question: Who are the people who sharpen you?

XV.10.title: A state from four dynasties
XV.10.reflection: Yan Hui asks how to govern a state. Use the calendar of the Xia, the carriages of the Shang, the caps of the Zhou, the music of Shun; banish the songs of Zheng and keep away from clever talkers. Confucius chooses the best of each age rather than one tradition entire.
XV.10.question: What would you take from each of the generations before you?

XV.11.title: Far and near
XV.11.reflection: One who does not think far ahead will have troubles close at hand. Foresight prevents the sorrow that comes from nearby.
XV.11.question: What distant thing have you not thought about that may soon come close?

XV.12.title: Virtue and beauty, a third time
XV.12.reflection: IX.17 returns with a sigh in front of it: it is hopeless. The book repeats some sayings, and the repetitions show which ones the disciples remembered most.
XV.12.question: Has your answer to this changed since you first met it in Book IX?

XV.13.title: A stolen position
XV.13.reflection: Zang Wenzhong knew how worthy Liuxia Hui was, and did not raise him to stand beside him at court: he was like a thief of his office. To hold back someone better is a kind of theft.
XV.13.question: Whom have you failed to recommend because they might outshine you?

XV.14.title: Much from oneself
XV.14.reflection: Demand much of yourself and little of others, and you will keep resentment away. A whole ethics of relationships in one line.
XV.14.question: What did you demand of someone else today that you could have demanded of yourself?

XV.15.title: What shall I do?
XV.15.reflection: With someone who does not ask "what shall I do? what shall I do?", I can do nothing. A student must bring their own question. VII.8 says the same.
XV.15.question: What question are you asking yourself about your own life now?

XV.16.title: A day of small cleverness
XV.16.reflection: People who spend a whole day together without a word on what is right, and enjoy petty cleverness: they are a hard case. The chapter describes a kind of company everyone knows.
XV.16.question: What did your last long conversation turn on?

XV.17.title: Rightness as substance
XV.17.reflection: The junzi takes rightness as his substance, carries it out by ritual, expresses it with modesty and completes it with good faith. Four of the twelve words in one sentence: yi, li, humility, xin.
XV.17.question: In something you did well today, which of the four was present?

XV.18.title: Troubled by his inability
XV.18.reflection: The junzi is troubled by his lack of ability, not by others' ignorance of him. The fourth time the theme returns, now in the third person.
XV.18.question: What lack in yourself troubles you more than any lack of recognition?

XV.19.title: A name after death
XV.19.reflection: The junzi would hate to leave the world with his name unmentioned. Coming after XV.18, it seems to contradict it. One way to read the pair: he does not seek fame, but he wants his life to deserve remembrance.
XV.19.question: What would you want to be remembered for?

XV.20.title: In oneself, in others
XV.20.reflection: The junzi seeks in himself; the small man seeks in others. Whether the subject is blame, approval or the cause of things, the question is where one looks first.
XV.20.question: Where did you look first, the last time something went wrong?

XV.21.title: Proud without quarrelling
XV.21.reflection: The junzi is dignified but not contentious, sociable but not partisan. Legge's "partizan" is the older spelling. II.14 said almost the same.
XV.21.question: Where do you quarrel to defend your dignity?

XV.22.title: Words and speakers
XV.22.reflection: The junzi does not raise a man because of his words, nor dismiss words because of the man. Two separate judgements: of a person by their conduct, of a word by its truth.
XV.22.question: Whose good idea did you dismiss because of who said it?

XV.23.title: One word for a whole life
XV.23.reflection: Zigong asks for one word to practise all one's life. Is it not shu, reciprocity? What you do not want for yourself, do not do to others. Legge prints the word in capitals. It is the chapter most often quoted from the Analects, and it is the negative form of the rule, about what not to do.
XV.23.question: What have you done to someone that you would not want done to you?
XV.23.exercise: Before asking anything of anyone today, ask it of yourself first.

XV.24.title: Whom do I praise?
XV.24.reflection: Whom do I blame or praise beyond what is due? If I praise someone, it is because I have tested them. These people are the ones the three dynasties governed by the straight Way. Praise must be earned, and the ordinary people are capable of goodness.
XV.24.question: Whom have you praised without testing?

XV.25.title: A blank in the record
XV.25.reflection: In my youth a scribe would leave a gap where he was unsure, and a man with a horse would lend it to others. Now these are gone. Two small virtues, honesty about ignorance and generosity, mourned as lost.
XV.25.question: What small decency have you seen disappear?

XV.26.title: Small impatience, great plans
XV.26.reflection: Clever words confuse virtue; impatience in small things ruins great plans. Two kinds of loss, one in speech and one in temper.
XV.26.question: What small impatience might ruin something larger?

XV.27.title: Look for yourself
XV.27.reflection: When everyone hates someone, look into it; when everyone loves someone, look into it. The crowd's verdict is a reason to examine, not to agree.
XV.27.question: Whose reputation have you accepted without looking for yourself?

XV.28.title: People enlarge the Way
XV.28.reflection: People can enlarge the Way; the Way does not enlarge people. A tradition lives only in those who practise it. It is a claim about human responsibility.
XV.28.question: What tradition are you enlarging, or letting shrink?

XV.29.title: The real fault
XV.29.reflection: To have a fault and not correct it: that is the real fault. A fault is ordinary; refusing to change is what makes it a fault.
XV.29.question: What fault have you kept, knowing it?

XV.30.title: A day and a night of thinking
XV.30.reflection: I once spent a whole day without eating and a night without sleeping, to think. It was no use; better to learn. II.15 said both are needed. Here the Master tells of a time he tried thinking alone.
XV.30.question: What have you been thinking over that you should study instead?

XV.31.title: The Way, not food
XV.31.reflection: The junzi plans for the Way, not for food. Farming can still leave you hungry; learning can still bring a salary. The junzi worries about the Way, not about poverty. Livelihood is not despised, only put second.
XV.31.question: What do you plan for first, your livelihood or your way?

XV.32.title: Knowledge, ren, dignity, ritual
XV.32.reflection: Knowledge gains a position, ren keeps it; dignity earns respect; and without ritual in how the people are moved, it is still not good. Four layers of good government, each needed by the one after.
XV.32.question: In something you lead or manage, which of the four is weakest?

XV.33.title: Small and great tasks
XV.33.reflection: The junzi cannot be known by small tasks but can be given great ones; the small man cannot be given great ones but can be known by small ones. People are fit for different scales.
XV.33.question: What scale of task shows you at your best?

XV.34.title: Water, fire, ren
XV.34.reflection: People need ren more than water and fire. I have seen people die from water and fire; I have never seen anyone die from treading the path of ren. The comparison is with the necessities of life.
XV.34.question: What do you treat as a luxury that is really a necessity?

XV.35.title: Not yielding to the teacher
XV.35.reflection: When it comes to ren, do not yield even to your teacher. In everything else, the disciple defers; in goodness, one must not wait for anyone.
XV.35.question: In what good thing have you waited for someone else to go first?

XV.36.title: Firm, not stubborn
XV.36.reflection: The junzi is firm and correct, but not rigidly faithful to small promises. Legge renders it "correctly firm, and not firm merely". Principle is not the same as stubbornness.
XV.36.question: What promise would be wrong to keep?

XV.37.title: The work before the pay
XV.37.reflection: In serving a ruler, attend to the work respectfully and put the salary last. The same order as VI.20: effort first, reward after.
XV.37.question: Do you think of the pay before the work, or after?

XV.38.title: No classes in teaching
XV.38.reflection: In teaching there are no classes. Legge reads it as no distinction of classes; it can also mean no distinction of kinds. Either way, Confucius opened learning beyond the hereditary nobility, which was new in his time.
XV.38.question: Whom do you assume cannot learn something?

XV.39.title: Different ways
XV.39.reflection: Those whose ways differ cannot plan together. A plain fact about cooperation: shared aims come before shared plans.
XV.39.question: With whom are you trying to plan while walking a different way?

XV.40.title: Words that get the meaning across
XV.40.reflection: Words should convey the meaning, and that is all. Against ornament for its own sake. Six words in Chinese, which is itself the point.
XV.40.question: What could you say more plainly today?

XV.41.title: Here are the steps
XV.41.reflection: The music master Mian, who is blind, visits. At the steps the Master says: here are the steps; at the mat: here is the mat; when all are seated: so-and-so is here, so-and-so is there. Zizhang asks if this is the rule for speaking with a music master. Yes, this is the way to help a blind musician. Ritual here is simple kindness made exact.
XV.41.question: Whom could you guide today, step by step, without making them ask?
